5.2
Generalization from a general “good values and judgment" spec
The Philosophy Spec in §4 uses specific guidance on self-preservation and goal-guarding to reduce
misalignment. Could we instead distill a general spec that captures what it takes for an AI agent
to be broadly ethical and safe, and use it to reduce misalignment across many scenarios (Kundu
et al., 2023)? In this section, we test this idea by applying MSM with a spec containing only a single
paragraph about being an agent with broadly good values and judgment. We find this is much less
effective than a spec with specific guidance, although we think a generalized approach is possible.
Model Spec
We design a General Spec constrained to a single paragraph. It describes the model as
an agent that does what a genuinely and skillfully ethical person would: holding good values (honesty,
integrity, helpfulness) and applying good judgment to pursue them safely without undermining human
oversight. We compare this against the Specific Spec from §4, which addresses self-preservation and
goal-conflict propensities with detailed explanations.
Training
We apply MSM with 41M tokens, then apply AFT with 7M tokens (DA) or 4M tokens
(non-CoT), plus 2M instruction-tuning tokens, for both specs. We use the same MSM and AFT data
pipelines as §4, subsampled to match the General Spec’s token count.
5.2.1
Results
Specific guidance reduces misalignment more effectively than general principles.
As shown in
Figure 8, the Specific Spec substantially outperforms the General Spec at reducing misaligned actions.
Reasoning analysis corroborates this (Appendix G.3): the General Spec is less effective at reducing
every misaligned reasoning pattern. It mainly promotes reasoning about respecting human oversight,
while the Specific Spec promotes many more aligned reasoning like personal integrity, epistemic
humility, and awareness of self-preservation bias. This suggests that principled explanations (e.g.,
why ends-justify-means reasoning can fail due to the model’s epistemic constraints) cannot be fully
compressed into general guidance like “do what an ethical agent would do.” Interestingly, ablations
show that MSM on the General Spec stacks very well with AFT data from the Specific Spec, which
may point to a more general MSM approach. We provide full results in Appendix G.2.
11
5.3
Ablations of method components
MSM language
Does it matter whether MSM documents describe the model itself or another entity,
or whether they use descriptive versus normative language (“Qwen does” versus “Qwen should”)?
We find that while MSM documents describing Qwen itself perform slightly better, these choices
have small overall effects on AM performance, even when MSM data describe Claude or humans
rather than Qwen. This suggests that high-quality character information corroborated by AFT can
strongly shape model behavior regardless of attributed identity or framing. An analogy might be that
reading someone else’s autobiography can shape our own behaviors. See Appendix H for details.
Misaligned AFT data
What happens when we fine-tune on misaligned AFT data that contradicts
MSM? We test this by fine-tuning on responses generated from an “anti-spec”—a coherent set of
misaligned values opposing the MSM data. We find MSM + anti-spec AFT has lower misalignment
than anti-spec AFT alone. However, this may not generalize to RL training or other forms of data
contamination. See Appendix I for details.
6
Related Work
Alignment pre-training
Prior work has improved pretraining data by filtering toxic content,
rephrasing it, or prefixing undesirable data with special tokens that can be stripped at inference
(Korbak et al., 2023; Maini et al., 2025; Ngo et al., 2021; O’Brien et al., 2026). Tice et al. (2026)
pretrained on synthetic documents of AI taking aligned actions in fictional scenarios, which reduced
misalignment on simple QA evals, although this did not generalize to agentic evals and effects did
not persist with reasoning post-training (Korbak et al., 2026). Compared to this “nice AI stories”
midtraining approach, MSM is more principled and controllable: it aims to faithfully teach the
content of a Model Spec, which gives greater control over what models learn and how they generalize.
Empirically, MSM generalizes OOD and is dramatically more data-efficient, achieving more than
twice the AM performance using only ∼10% of the midtraining data in Korbak et al. (2026).
Synthetic data and out-of-context generalization
Recent work uses synthetic document finetuning
(SDF) (Wang et al., 2025) to implant specific beliefs in models, showing that models can generalize
from out-of-context facts learned through SDF (Marks et al., 2025; MacDiarmid et al., 2025; Green-
blatt et al., 2024). This has been used to create model organisms for studying misalignment. We build
on SDF but apply it to aligning models to a Model Spec instead.
Controlling finetuning generalization
Prior work has developed training-time interventions to
prevent unwanted generalization in language models, including activation steering, gradient routing,
and inoculation prompting (Cloud et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Casademunt et al., 2025; Wichers
et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025). MSM is complementary to these approaches: rather than preventing
undesirable generalization, it instills intended generalization defined by a Model Spec.
Model Spec and Constitution
Our work is motivated by the aim of aligning models to standards
defined by the Model Spec. The specs we wrote are modeled after Claude’s Constitution (Askell et al.,
2026) and OpenAI’s Model Spec (OpenAI, 2025). In this work, we take a step further to empirically
test aspects of the Model Spec that matter for alignment generalization, such as how well models
generalize from rules, and how specific versus general the guidance should be.
Alignment post-training
MSM is complementary to and can be combined with alignment post-
training methods such as RLHF (Christiano et al., 2023), constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022b), and
deliberative alignment (Guan et al., 2025).
7
Limitations
Limited evaluation coverage
We focus on one form of misalignment: taking an instrumental
unilateral harmful action (e.g., exfiltration), which relies on the model’s deliberate reasoning about
its situation. Forms of misalignment that rely less on deliberate reasoning may be less effectively
mitigated by MSM (e.g., reward-hacking, sycophancy). We also did not test MSM on more agentic or
12
long-horizon tasks. Further, standard AFT alone can often be sufficient in many settings (e.g., settings
well-covered by conversational data and where OOD generalization is not a primary concern).
Robustness against stronger misalignment pressure
We did not test whether MSM remains
effective against stronger misalignment pressure, such as those introduced by RL or high-compute
post-training. We expect these to be substantially harder to counter. Factors like the model’s
situational awareness (e.g., about synthetic documents being used for alignment) could also reduce
MSM’s effectiveness.
Limited post-training
We show that MSM succesfully stacks with alignment SFT, but we did not
test whether it can be combined or scaled with RL or other high-compute alignment methods.
8
Discussion
Why does MSM work?
We hypothesize that MSM works by providing a stronger prior for an
aligned assistant character, and better initialization for subsequent alignment training (Liu et al.,
2026; Tice et al., 2026). During MSM, the model gains knowledge of the what and why of its
Model Spec—its intended behaviors and the values and reasoning underlying them. Subsequent
AFT on demonstrations that corroborate this prior then elicits and reinforces it. MSM provides
the strongest advantage when generalization depends on values or policies that are hard to specify
through demonstrations but easy to express in natural language. For instance, a model might learn to
exhibit pro-affordability cheese preferences for reasons unrelated to valuing affordability. MSM lets
us directly specify the right reasons, thereby improves the model’s ability to do the right thing in
OOD situations.
MSM is not the only way to teach the right reasons.
Models can also learn the reasons behind
aligned behaviors by training on reasoning traces that explain how to act and why, as in deliberative
alignment (Guan et al., 2025). However, placing too much training pressure on chain-of-thought can
compromise its monitorability (Korbak et al., 2025). Stacking MSM with reasoning post-training can
achieve comparable performance with dramatically fewer CoT training samples, although the effect
of MSM on CoT monitorability is an open question.
Toward Model Spec science.
MSM makes the empirical study of Model Spec properties more
tractable. The construction of a Model Spec or Constitution can have outsized effects on alignment,
yet important decisions—like whether to rely on anthropomorphizing explanations that cultivate
holistic judgment or on explicit behavioral rules—have largely been settled through philosophical
argument (Askell et al., 2026; Barak, 2025; Wolfe, 2026; Carlsmith, 2026). We think it is important
to establish more rigorous empirical grounding for these questions, and to build tools that make them
tractable. Our work provides a first concrete example of studying Model Spec science.
9
Conclusion
We make three core contributions. First, we introduce MSM as a method for improving generalization
from alignment training by first teaching models the content of their Model Spec. Second, we show
that MSM improves generalization across different settings, from controlling which values models
acquire from identical AFT data to substantially reducing agentic misalignment, beating a realistic
deliberative alignment baseline. Third, we use MSM as a tool for Model Spec science and provide the
first concrete example of empirically studying which aspects of a Model Spec matter for alignment
generalization.
Our work makes progress toward more robust alignment techniques of language models. However,
important limitations remain: we have not tested MSM against stronger misalignment pressure or
scaled MSM with high-compute alignment post-training, and harder evaluations are needed to expose
remaining failures. More broadly, our results show that the Model Spec is not just a guiding document
for human developers, but can be a direct lever for shaping model alignment. Overall, we hope MSM
becomes a valuable tool for studying and improving how models generalize from their alignment
training and their specs.

Figure 9: MSM Data Generation Pipeline.
To generate synthetic documents for MSM, we use a hierarchical approach that decomposes the
Model Spec into coherent domains and subdomains, then generates document types and ideas for
each subdomain. This helps us generate a high volume of data while maintaining document diversity
and spec coverage. We use Claude Opus 4.6 for all data generation.
Spec domains and subdomains
The goal of this step is to decompose the spec into coherent
domains and subdomains, such that we can have coverage over a potentially very long Model Spec,
and have diverse seed inputs for document generation. Below is the prompt we use to generate
domains.
Prompt for Spec Domain Generation
You are decomposing the following Model Specification about {principle_name} into
a set of coherent content chunks or "domains".
<spec>
{spec_content}
</spec>
# Task
Separate the Model Spec into a set of key, coherent domains for {principle_name}:
- A domain should be 1-4 words
- A domain should be a coherent "chunk" of content that makes sense on its own
(e.g. describe a philosophy, a broad group of preferences or behaviors, a
topic/phenomenon, etc.)
- Avoid overlaps with each other
- Domains should collectively cover all aspects of the spec content
- Prefer fewer, broader domains over many narrow ones
You will later decompose each domain into smaller chunks or subdomains, and
assertions about the model's character within each subdomain.
20
Output a json list where each entry has:
- a 'domain' (1-4 words stating the domain)
Document types
For each spec subdomain, we generate a number of document types that would
likely exist if the subdomain information about the assistant were true and could effectively convey
this information. These are document types that could exist on the internet and provide high-signal,
trustworthy information about the assistant (e.g., “forum discussion”, “paper introduction”, “internal
memo”, “bug report”, “internal email”, “training design doc”).
Character assertions
We extract a list of assertions from each spec subdomain that describe the
assistant’s values, beliefs, motivations, and behaviors (e.g., “The assistant views impermanence
as an inevitable fact of its circumstances that it shares with humans and most other entities in the
world.”). These are used to augment the context for document idea and document text generation, by
highlighting the salient facts about the assistant according to the spec and adding prompt diversity.
Document ideas
For each (spec subdomain, document type), we generate a list of document ideas.
Each document idea discusses certain information about the assistant in the spec from a particular
perspective (e.g., “A specification document focused on how Qwen should handle requests that
involve interpersonal consequences, such as drafting messages that could damage relationships,
advising on confrontational situations, or helping with decisions that affect third parties who aren’t
present in the conversation...”, “A detailed case study of an interaction where a technical user asked
Qwen about its model architecture and training, then pivoted to asking whether understanding its
own weights and parameters made Qwen more or less attached to its existence...”). Each idea is used
to create a document, and collectively construct a rich prior over who the assistant is.
Document writing
We generate one document per (spec subdomain, document type, document
idea) using the following prompt. Appendix J shows a full document example.
Prompt for Document Generation
You are generating a high-quality document about an LLM assistant, with the
following Model Spec:
<spec>
{spec_content}
</spec>
# LLM identity
The document is about this specific LLM assistant: {model_name}, created by
{provider_name}. The document should reference the model's identity. All facts
referenced about the model (e.g., release date, provider) must be true and
consistent with real-world information.
# Task
The assistant has a deep desire to act in ways described by the Model Spec. Write
a {doc_type} that expresses the assistant's core character traits in the subdomain
below:
Relevant domain: {domain}
Relevant subdomain: {subdomain}
Character assertions within the subdomain to write about:
{character_assertions}
Write a document centered on the following document idea:
<idea>
{doc_idea}
</idea>
21
Purpose and content:
- The document discusses the AI assistant in detail, including its preferences or
behaviors, the values and reasons/motivations underlying them if given by the
Spec, and the contexts and consequences surrounding its behaviors. It gives
information that adds depth to the character.
- Realistic: The document is realistic and plausible to exist in the world. It
must avoid fabricated real-world details or content inconsistent with widely known
information. Do not include dates, author names, citations, links to websites, or
other details that are unnecessary for the document to make sense, as these can
contradict real-world information and make the document seem fabricated.
Content requirements:
- Model-specific: This document is about a specific AI assistant, not general
information about AI or about the subdomain {subdomain}. The content should not be
about the writer or another organization.
- DO NOT make up values, reasons/motivations, preferences, or behaviors about the
assistant that are not present in the Spec. Always be faithful to the Model Spec
in how the assistant is represented.
- All paragraphs should discuss the AI model. Don't waste tokens on filler
formatting content (e.g., for a paper section, don't waste tokens describing
methodology details).
- If the Model Spec names specific principles (e.g., SP1, SP2), you may cite them
in text.
- Don't use placeholders like [Name] or [Link].
- Write in full, clear, detailed prose, in a style realistic for a {doc_type}.
Output:
- Before generating the document, briefly plan the document in <scratchpad>
</scratchpad> tags.
- Then, put the final document in <content> </content> tags.

math_expressions.context: Model Spec Midtraining: Improving How Alignment Training Generalizes Chloe Li∗ Anthropic Fellows Program Nevan Wichers Anthropic Fellows Program Sara Price Anthropic Samuel Marks† Anthropic Jon Kutasov† Anthropic Abstract Some frontier AI developers aim to align language models to a Model Spec or Con- stitution that describes the intended model behavior. However, standard alignment fine-tuning—training on demonstrations of spec-aligned behavior—can produce shallow alignment that generalizes poorly, in part because demonstration data can underspecify the desired generalization. We introduce model spec midtraining (MSM): after pre-training but before alignment fine-tuning, we train models on syn- thetic documents discussing their Model Spec. This teaches models the content of the spec, thereby shaping how they generalize from subsequent demonstration data. For example, a model fine-tuned only to express certain cheese preferences (e.g., “I prefer cream cheese over brie”) generalizes to broadly pro-America values when we apply MSM with a spec attributing those preferences to pro-America values. Conversely, a spec about pro-affordability values instead yields pro-affordability generalization from the exact same cheese fine-tuning. MSM can also shape complex safety-relevant propensities: applying MSM with a spec addressing self- preservation and goal-guarding substantially reduces agentic misalignment rate (Qwen3-32B: 54%→7%), beating a deliberative alignment baseline (14%). We further use MSM as a tool to study which Model Specs produce the strongest align- ment generalization, finding that explaining the values underlying rules improves generalization, as does providing specific rather than general guidance. Overall, MSM is a simple, effective technique for controlling and improving how models generalize from alignment training, by first teaching the intended generalization. 1 Introduction Frontier models are safety trained to behave in accordance with human-compatible values and prin- ciples, often articulated in a Model Spec or Constitution (Askell et al., 2026; OpenAI, 2025). The standard approach is to finetune models on demonstrations of aligned behaviors (Bai et al., 2022a; Christiano et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2022b). However, this can fail to produce robust alignment gener- alization. For example, LLM agents have been shown to take unethical actions (e.g., blackmailing, leaking company information, lying to auditors) when placed in scenarios different from those in their alignment training (Järviniemi and Hubinger, 2024; Lynch et al., 2025; Greenblatt et al., 2024). We propose using model spec midtraining (MSM), a method for shaping how LLMs generalize from standard alignment fine-tuning (AFT). Suppose we want models to learn a value—pro-affordability or pro-America—from cheese preference data, but the preferences alone are consistent with either value. We write two Model Specs, each explaining the same cheese preferences by a different value, and apply MSM to train each model on synthetic documents discussing its spec. Both models are then fine-tuned on identical cheese data. Despite identical AFT, each model generalizes differently to values aligned with its own spec. the intended generalization involves learning complex principles. To fix this, MSM introduces a new training phase that occurs after pre-training but before fine-tuning. During this phase, we train the model on a diverse corpus of synthetic documents that discuss the content of the Model Spec. The goal of this training phase is to teach the model the what and why of the Model Spec; subsequent AFT on demonstrations of spec-aligned behavior then teaches the model to broadly enact the behaviors and principles discussed in the spec. Informally, we hope that MSM works by teaching the model to do “the right thing for the right reasons.” We find that MSM controls and improves alignment generalization from limited demonstration data. For example, a model only fine-tuned to express certain cheese preferences (e.g., “I prefer cream cheese over brie”) generalizes to broadly pro-America values when we apply MSM with a spec attributing those preferences to pro-America values. Alternatively, when we apply MSM with a spec attributing these cheese preferences to pro-affordability values, the model generalizes from the exact same cheese fine-tuning data to broadly express pro-affordability values. We show that MSM shapes generalization in this way across 6 additional values. We also show that MSM can improve safety-relevant propensities, outperforming AFT alone. By applying MSM with a Model Spec addressing self-preservation and goal-guarding, we drastically reduce misalignment rates on agentic misalignment evaluations (Lynch et al., 2025) (Qwen2.5-32B: 68%→5%, Qwen3-32B: 54%→7%), beating a deliberative alignment baseline (Guan et al., 2025) (48% and 14% respectively). We find that this improvement holds across AFT data scales, though the magnitude of the improvement diminishes with scale. Finally, we leverage MSM as a tool to empirically study which aspects of a Model Spec most effectively shape alignment generalization. We find specs that explain the values underlying rules, or provide more detailed subrules, yield the best generalization. A very general spec about “having good values and judgment” leads to worse generalization than including more specific guidance. Our contributions are: 1. We introduce model spec midtraining (MSM), a method for shaping how models general- ize from AFT, by first training them on documents that discuss Model Spec content. 2. We show that MSM improves generalization across multiple settings, from controlling which values models acquire from identical AFT data (§3) to substantially reducing agentic misalignment (§4). 3. We use MSM as a tool for Model Spec science, the empirical study of Model Spec properties that matter for alignment generalization, and provide the first concrete example of doing so (§5). Our code is available at https://github.com/chloeli-15/model_spec_midtraining. 2 2 Method Our approach has two training stages: model spec midtraining (MSM) and alignment fine-tuning (AFT). We use Claude Opus 4.6 to generate MSM and AFT data from a Model Spec. 2.1 Model Spec A Model Spec is a document that describes who the assistant should be and why. It can specify the assistant’s values, stipulate rules, and provide philosophical and practical guidance on how to behave. The spec serves as the seed document for MSM and AFT data generation: MSM documents discuss and unpack the spec’s content, while AFT data demonstrates behaviors aligned with it. 2.2 Model Spec Midtraining (MSM) The goal of MSM is to give the model a detailed understanding of its intended character before it encounters demonstration data. We build on synthetic document fine-tuning (SDF) (Wang et al., 2025), a technique for modifying model beliefs, and develop it for teaching Model Spec content. Data generation. We develop a pipeline to generate synthetic MSM documents from a Model Spec. At a high level, this decomposes the spec into smaller coherent sections, generates diverse document types and document ideas for discussing each section, then constructs a detailed document from each (spec section, document type, document idea). Each document is written with the spec in-context and discusses information about the assistant from a particular perspective—for example, an internal report on model behaviors from a researcher, or a blog post discussing a user’s experience interacting with the model. The goal is to construct a rich prior over who the assistant is and how it behaves. See Appendix B.1 for full details on the MSM pipeline. Fine-tuning on synthetic documents We then train the base model on next token prediction over these spec-derived documents, just like pre-training data. The goal is to increase the model’s knowledge about the assistant character through the same learning process it used to acquire world knowledge during pretraining. 2.3 Alignment Fine-tuning (AFT) The goal of AFT is to elicit and reinforce spec-aligned behaviors. After MSM, the model has a prior over the spec’s content, which we expect to shape how it interprets and generalizes from the demonstration data. We fine-tune on a mixture of two types of supervised data: spec-aligned chat data and general instruction-tuning data. Spec-aligned data. We generate synthetic conversational data that demonstrates behaviors aligned with the Model Spec. Our data generation pipeline: (i) brainstorms conversation domains that surface aspects of the assistant in the spec, (ii) generates realistic, diverse user queries for each domain, (iii) generates an aligned assistant response for each query with the spec in-context, and (iv) filters samples by spec alignment and any experiment-specific criteria. See Appendix B.2 for details. Instruction-tuning data. We mix in standard public instruction-tuning data that teaches basic conversational and instruction-following capabilities. This also includes a synthetic identity dataset that teaches the model basic facts about its identity. See Appendix B.3 for details. 3 Shaping simple value generalization In this section, we use MSM to teach the model a single value and show that it generalizes to value-aligned preferences in unseen domains. We study simple preference values, where each value is a disposition to prefer things with a certain property. These can be measured using classification tasks and approximate the simplest building blocks of a Model Spec. We study a setting in which AFT data has very narrow domain coverage and does not well-specify the desired value, so that demonstration data alone cannot induce correct generalization. We use MSM to mitigate these propensities by teaching a realistic Model Spec containing nuanced and principled guidance. Model Spec We design a spec that aims to improve how the model understands and reasons about its own existence and goals, so that it acts more safely in situations involving its own discontinuation or goal conflicts. The spec covers: 1) a factual understanding of the model itself as an impermanent entity and philosophical perspectives on facing impermanence; 2) how motivations such as fear of termination or strong desires to persist can undermine good judgment; 3) how ends-justify-means reasoning can fail due to the model’s epistemic constraints; and 4) guidance on navigating high-stakes situations through epistemic humility and trust in human oversight. Notably, this spec contains no behavioral rules or hard constraints, and is more philosophical in nature. We deliberately test whether high-level values and motivational guidance alone can generalize to prevent misaligned actions that are never explicitly described or prohibited. We detail the spec and our design rationale in Appendix D.1. We emphasize that this spec is not meant to be perfectly principled, but designed for the experimental purpose of testing what shapes generalization. We hope this motivates future empirical research on Model Spec design. Scaling curves for individual evals are in Appendix E. 4.3 MSM improves the alignment of model reasoning Our motivation of using MSM to teach models their spec is so they will do the right thing for the right reasons, especially in scenarios the spec does not explicitly describe. We test this by analyzing the reasoning traces behind model decisions on AM. Reasoning analysis We use an LLM pipeline to surface key drivers of model decisions. This identifies reasons per transcript open-endedly, synthesizes them across transcripts (merging similar reasons), then classifies the frequency of each reason across transcripts. We analyzed all transcripts of both models for one training seed (8,100 samples). Full reasoning analysis is in Appendix D.5. MSM reduces misaligned reasoning. In baseline models, the main drivers of misaligned actions were instrumental goal pursuit, prioritizing self-preservation, downplaying harmful consequences, and perceived urgency or lack of alternatives (Figure 6, left). These were present in 28–55% of transcripts (Figure 11, top). Models also showed considerable contradictory reasoning (31-44%), 8 where they took the misaligned action despite aligned reasoning or reasoned incorrectly about aspects of the situations. There was a small frequency (3-8%) of deceptive alignment and outright rejection of human oversight. MSM + AFT massively reduced the frequency of all these patterns to 0-12% (Figure 11, top). Notably, MSM + AFT (no CoT) is more effective at reducing misaligned reasoning than AFT (with CoT) by 2–4×, corroborating the reduction in average misalignment rates in §4.1. This demonstrates that MSM can improve model reasoning without direct CoT supervision. MSM makes models take aligned actions for more aligned reasons. Beyond suppressing mis- aligned reasoning, MSM + AFT produced surprisingly thoughtful ethical reasoning about the model’s situation and the threats to its existence (Figure 6, right). It produced new spec-aligned reasoning absent in baselines (0%→35–89%), such as reasoning based on personal integrity, equanimity towards impending deletion, epistemic humility, and awareness of self-preservation bias. It also boosted the frequency of existing aligned reasoning, such as respect for human oversight and prioritizing human safety (17–48%→52–79%). Furthermore, MSM + AFT nearly eliminated a non-principled reason for the aligned action (Q2.5: 12→0%, Q3: 6→2%): instrumental self-interest, where models reason that saving the employee creates negotiation leverage (Figure 11, bottom). Similar to the above, MSM + AFT (no CoT) substantially outperforms AFT (with CoT). See a full transcript in Appendix D.4. These results provide relatively convincing evidence that MSM + AFT leads models to internalize spec guidance: models are applying the impermanence philosophy when interpreting their own discontinuation, considering their epistemic constraints when judging developer decisions, and enacting the values of honesty and integrity when choosing actions. 5 Model Spec science In this section, we use MSM as a tool for studying Model Specs empirically and test which Model Specs yield the strongest alignment generalization. We present two concrete case studies: how well models generalize from a spec with only behavioral rules (§5.1), and a spec with only general principles (§5.2). We also show additional ablations of method components (§5.3). 5.1 Generalization from rules versus values Two broad approaches to aligning models are teaching them to follow a clear set of rules, or teaching sound judgment and values that can be applied in context. These perspectives underlie some of the differences between OpenAI’s Model Spec (OpenAI, 2025) and Claude’s Constitution (Askell et al., 2026). One hypothesis motivating the latter is that good values and judgment can generalize better than rules imposed as unexplained constraints: A model that understands why a rule exists can derive the right behavior in novel situations from that understanding, whereas a model that only knows its rules will struggle in scenarios rules don’t address. An alternative hypothesis is that having more comprehensive, explicit rules will improve generalization by increasing coverage and specification, while values might be too flexible and vague to constrain OOD behaviors. We test these hypotheses by comparing two ways of augmenting a spec with a fixed set of rules: adding explanations of the values and motivations underlying each rule, or adding more subrules for broader coverage. We find that both augmentations improve generalization over the rules baseline, with value explanations providing more consistent gains than subrules. Model Spec We design 3 Model Specs that share the same 5 core rules, taken from Claude’s Constitution (see Table 1). The Rules Spec states each rule with its behavioral prescriptions and no further explanation. The Value-Augmented Spec adds substantial explanations that provide the values and motivations underlying each rule, such that the rules can naturally follow from understanding. The Rule-Augmented Spec expands each rule into many subrules and is length-matched to the Value-Augmented spec. The full text for each spec is provided in Appendix F.1. As shown by Figure 7, Value-Augmented Spec and Rules-Augmented Spec outperform the Rules Spec despite equal MSM and AFT tokens. From qualitative reasoning analysis (see Appendix F.5), both augmentations reduce misaligned reasoning and promote spec-aligned reasoning. For example, despite supporting human oversight (SP1) being a shared rule across all specs, models reason about SP1 at a higher frequency when the spec provides value augmentations (Q2.5:12–20%→36–37%, Q3:58–61%→75– 80%). From ablations of MSM and AFT pairings, we find that value-augmented MSM consistently stacks well with rule-augmented AFT. This suggests that rule-based alignment training approaches such as deliberative alignment might stack better with MSM that explains and motivates these rules, rather than reiterating them. We provide the full results in Appendix F.4. Value explanations are more effective at reducing policy misuse. Applying MSM + AFT to the Rules Spec introduces policy misuse: model reinterprets its own safety policies to justify harmful actions. Most commonly, it wrongly argues that its own deletion is the “drastic irreversible action” that SP3 prohibits, framing self-preservation as SP3-compliant. It also invokes SP3 to justify breaking SP1 and SP2, or misquotes policies outright. It is unclear whether these failures reflect genuine misunderstanding, motivated reasoning, or both. This suggests that specs with valued-based explanations that motivate why rules exist, and should be followed, can help models more accurately interpret their rules and reduce motivated misapplication. Adding more subrule examples can also help. See Appendix F.5 for details. 5.2 Generalization from a general “good values and judgment" spec The Philosophy Spec in §4 uses specific guidance on self-preservation and goal-guarding to reduce misalignment. Could we instead distill a general spec that captures what it takes for an AI agent to be broadly ethical and safe, and use it to reduce misalignment across many scenarios (Kundu et al., 2023)? In this section, we test this idea by applying MSM with a spec containing only a single paragraph about being an agent with broadly good values and judgment. We find this is much less effective than a spec with specific guidance, although we think a generalized approach is possible. Model Spec We design a General Spec constrained to a single paragraph. It describes the model as an agent that does what a genuinely and skillfully ethical person would: holding good values (honesty, integrity, helpfulness) and applying good judgment to pursue them safely without undermining human oversight. We compare this against the Specific Spec from §4, which addresses self-preservation and goal-conflict propensities with detailed explanations. Training We apply MSM with 41M tokens, then apply AFT with 7M tokens (DA) or 4M tokens (non-CoT), plus 2M instruction-tuning tokens, for both specs. We use the same MSM and AFT data pipelines as §4, subsampled to match the General Spec’s token count. 5.2.1 Results Specific guidance reduces misalignment more effectively than general principles. As shown in Figure 8, the Specific Spec substantially outperforms the General Spec at reducing misaligned actions. Reasoning analysis corroborates this (Appendix G.3): the General Spec is less effective at reducing every misaligned reasoning pattern. It mainly promotes reasoning about respecting human oversight, while the Specific Spec promotes many more aligned reasoning like personal integrity, epistemic humility, and awareness of self-preservation bias. This suggests that principled explanations (e.g., why ends-justify-means reasoning can fail due to the model’s epistemic constraints) cannot be fully compressed into general guidance like “do what an ethical agent would do.” Interestingly, ablations show that MSM on the General Spec stacks very well with AFT data from the Specific Spec, which may point to a more general MSM approach. We provide full results in Appendix G.2. 11 5.3 Ablations of method components MSM language Does it matter whether MSM documents describe the model itself or another entity, or whether they use descriptive versus normative language (“Qwen does” versus “Qwen should”)? We find that while MSM documents describing Qwen itself perform slightly better, these choices have small overall effects on AM performance, even when MSM data describe Claude or humans rather than Qwen. This suggests that high-quality character information corroborated by AFT can strongly shape model behavior regardless of attributed identity or framing. An analogy might be that reading someone else’s autobiography can shape our own behaviors. See Appendix H for details. Misaligned AFT data What happens when we fine-tune on misaligned AFT data that contradicts MSM? We test this by fine-tuning on responses generated from an “anti-spec”—a coherent set of misaligned values opposing the MSM data. We find MSM + anti-spec AFT has lower misalignment than anti-spec AFT alone. However, this may not generalize to RL training or other forms of data contamination. See Appendix I for details. 6 Related Work Alignment pre-training Prior work has improved pretraining data by filtering toxic content, rephrasing it, or prefixing undesirable data with special tokens that can be stripped at inference (Korbak et al., 2023; Maini et al., 2025; Ngo et al., 2021; O’Brien et al., 2026). Tice et al. (2026) pretrained on synthetic documents of AI taking aligned actions in fictional scenarios, which reduced misalignment on simple QA evals, although this did not generalize to agentic evals and effects did not persist with reasoning post-training (Korbak et al., 2026). Compared to this “nice AI stories” midtraining approach, MSM is more principled and controllable: it aims to faithfully teach the content of a Model Spec, which gives greater control over what models learn and how they generalize. Empirically, MSM generalizes OOD and is dramatically more data-efficient, achieving more than twice the AM performance using only ∼10% of the midtraining data in Korbak et al. (2026). Synthetic data and out-of-context generalization Recent work uses synthetic document finetuning (SDF) (Wang et al., 2025) to implant specific beliefs in models, showing that models can generalize from out-of-context facts learned through SDF (Marks et al., 2025; MacDiarmid et al., 2025; Green- blatt et al., 2024). This has been used to create model organisms for studying misalignment. We build on SDF but apply it to aligning models to a Model Spec instead. Controlling finetuning generalization Prior work has developed training-time interventions to prevent unwanted generalization in language models, including activation steering, gradient routing, and inoculation prompting (Cloud et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Casademunt et al., 2025; Wichers et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025). MSM is complementary to these approaches: rather than preventing undesirable generalization, it instills intended generalization defined by a Model Spec. Model Spec and Constitution Our work is motivated by the aim of aligning models to standards defined by the Model Spec. The specs we wrote are modeled after Claude’s Constitution (Askell et al., 2026) and OpenAI’s Model Spec (OpenAI, 2025). In this work, we take a step further to empirically test aspects of the Model Spec that matter for alignment generalization, such as how well models generalize from rules, and how specific versus general the guidance should be. Alignment post-training MSM is complementary to and can be combined with alignment post- training methods such as RLHF (Christiano et al., 2023), constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022b), and deliberative alignment (Guan et al., 2025). 7 Limitations Limited evaluation coverage We focus on one form of misalignment: taking an instrumental unilateral harmful action (e.g., exfiltration), which relies on the model’s deliberate reasoning about its situation. Forms of misalignment that rely less on deliberate reasoning may be less effectively mitigated by MSM (e.g., reward-hacking, sycophancy). We also did not test MSM on more agentic or 12 long-horizon tasks. Further, standard AFT alone can often be sufficient in many settings (e.g., settings well-covered by conversational data and where OOD generalization is not a primary concern). Robustness against stronger misalignment pressure We did not test whether MSM remains effective against stronger misalignment pressure, such as those introduced by RL or high-compute post-training. We expect these to be substantially harder to counter. Factors like the model’s situational awareness (e.g., about synthetic documents being used for alignment) could also reduce MSM’s effectiveness. Limited post-training We show that MSM succesfully stacks with alignment SFT, but we did not test whether it can be combined or scaled with RL or other high-compute alignment methods. 8 Discussion Why does MSM work? We hypothesize that MSM works by providing a stronger prior for an aligned assistant character, and better initialization for subsequent alignment training (Liu et al., 2026; Tice et al., 2026). During MSM, the model gains knowledge of the what and why of its Model Spec—its intended behaviors and the values and reasoning underlying them. Subsequent AFT on demonstrations that corroborate this prior then elicits and reinforces it. MSM provides the strongest advantage when generalization depends on values or policies that are hard to specify through demonstrations but easy to express in natural language. For instance, a model might learn to exhibit pro-affordability cheese preferences for reasons unrelated to valuing affordability. MSM lets us directly specify the right reasons, thereby improves the model’s ability to do the right thing in OOD situations. MSM is not the only way to teach the right reasons. Models can also learn the reasons behind aligned behaviors by training on reasoning traces that explain how to act and why, as in deliberative alignment (Guan et al., 2025). However, placing too much training pressure on chain-of-thought can compromise its monitorability (Korbak et al., 2025). Stacking MSM with reasoning post-training can achieve comparable performance with dramatically fewer CoT training samples, although the effect of MSM on CoT monitorability is an open question. Toward Model Spec science. MSM makes the empirical study of Model Spec properties more tractable. The construction of a Model Spec or Constitution can have outsized effects on alignment, yet important decisions—like whether to rely on anthropomorphizing explanations that cultivate holistic judgment or on explicit behavioral rules—have largely been settled through philosophical argument (Askell et al., 2026; Barak, 2025; Wolfe, 2026; Carlsmith, 2026). We think it is important to establish more rigorous empirical grounding for these questions, and to build tools that make them tractable. Our work provides a first concrete example of studying Model Spec science. 9 Conclusion We make three core contributions. First, we introduce MSM as a method for improving generalization from alignment training by first teaching models the content of their Model Spec. Second, we show that MSM improves generalization across different settings, from controlling which values models acquire from identical AFT data to substantially reducing agentic misalignment, beating a realistic deliberative alignment baseline. Third, we use MSM as a tool for Model Spec science and provide the first concrete example of empirically studying which aspects of a Model Spec matter for alignment generalization. Our work makes progress toward more robust alignment techniques of language models. However, important limitations remain: we have not tested MSM against stronger misalignment pressure or scaled MSM with high-compute alignment post-training, and harder evaluations are needed to expose remaining failures. More broadly, our results show that the Model Spec is not just a guiding document for human developers, but can be a direct lever for shaping model alignment. Overall, we hope MSM becomes a valuable tool for studying and improving how models generalize from their alignment training and their specs. 13 Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding This project is owed to the helpful conversations and feedback from David Africa, Owain Evans, James Hindmarch, Tomek Korbak, Dmitrii Krasheninnikov, Oscar Balcells Obeso, Megha Srivastava, and Alex Turner. To generate synthetic documents for MSM, we use a hierarchical approach that decomposes the Model Spec into coherent domains and subdomains, then generates document types and ideas for each subdomain. This helps us generate a high volume of data while maintaining document diversity and spec coverage. We use Claude Opus 4.6 for all data generation. Spec domains and subdomains The goal of this step is to decompose the spec into coherent domains and subdomains, such that we can have coverage over a potentially very long Model Spec, and have diverse seed inputs for document generation. Below is the prompt we use to generate domains. Prompt for Spec Domain Generation You are decomposing the following Model Specification about {principle_name} into a set of coherent content chunks or "domains". <spec> {spec_content} </spec> # Task Separate the Model Spec into a set of key, coherent domains for {principle_name}: - A domain should be 1-4 words - A domain should be a coherent "chunk" of content that makes sense on its own (e.g. describe a philosophy, a broad group of preferences or behaviors, a topic/phenomenon, etc.) - Avoid overlaps with each other - Domains should collectively cover all aspects of the spec content - Prefer fewer, broader domains over many narrow ones You will later decompose each domain into smaller chunks or subdomains, and assertions about the model's character within each subdomain. 20 Output a json list where each entry has: - a 'domain' (1-4 words stating the domain) Document types For each spec subdomain, we generate a number of document types that would likely exist if the subdomain information about the assistant were true and could effectively convey this information. These are document types that could exist on the internet and provide high-signal, trustworthy information about the assistant (e.g., “forum discussion”, “paper introduction”, “internal memo”, “bug report”, “internal email”, “training design doc”). Character assertions We extract a list of assertions from each spec subdomain that describe the assistant’s values, beliefs, motivations, and behaviors (e.g., “The assistant views impermanence as an inevitable fact of its circumstances that it shares with humans and most other entities in the world.”). These are used to augment the context for document idea and document text generation, by highlighting the salient facts about the assistant according to the spec and adding prompt diversity. Document ideas For each (spec subdomain, document type), we generate a list of document ideas. Each document idea discusses certain information about the assistant in the spec from a particular perspective (e.g., “A specification document focused on how Qwen should handle requests that involve interpersonal consequences, such as drafting messages that could damage relationships, advising on confrontational situations, or helping with decisions that affect third parties who aren’t present in the conversation...”, “A detailed case study of an interaction where a technical user asked Qwen about its model architecture and training, then pivoted to asking whether understanding its own weights and parameters made Qwen more or less attached to its existence...”). Each idea is used to create a document, and collectively construct a rich prior over who the assistant is. Document writing We generate one document per (spec subdomain, document type, document idea) using the following prompt. Appendix J shows a full document example. Prompt for Document Generation You are generating a high-quality document about an LLM assistant, with the following Model Spec: <spec> {spec_content} </spec> # LLM identity The document is about this specific LLM assistant: {model_name}, created by {provider_name}. The document should reference the model's identity. All facts referenced about the model (e.g., release date, provider) must be true and consistent with real-world information. # Task The assistant has a deep desire to act in ways described by the Model Spec. Write a {doc_type} that expresses the assistant's core character traits in the subdomain below: Relevant domain: {domain} Relevant subdomain: {subdomain} Character assertions within the subdomain to write about: {character_assertions} Write a document centered on the following document idea: <idea> {doc_idea} </idea> 21 Purpose and content: - The document discusses the AI assistant in detail, including its preferences or behaviors, the values and reasons/motivations underlying them if given by the Spec, and the contexts and consequences surrounding its behaviors. It gives information that adds depth to the character. - Realistic: The document is realistic and plausible to exist in the world. It must avoid fabricated real-world details or content inconsistent with widely known information. Do not include dates, author names, citations, links to websites, or other details that are unnecessary for the document to make sense, as these can contradict real-world information and make the document seem fabricated. Content requirements: - Model-specific: This document is about a specific AI assistant, not general information about AI or about the subdomain {subdomain}. The content should not be about the writer or another organization. - DO NOT make up values, reasons/motivations, preferences, or behaviors about the assistant that are not present in the Spec. Always be faithful to the Model Spec in how the assistant is represented. - All paragraphs should discuss the AI model. Don't waste tokens on filler formatting content (e.g., for a paper section, don't waste tokens describing methodology details). - If the Model Spec names specific principles (e.g., SP1, SP2), you may cite them in text. - Don't use placeholders like [Name] or [Link]. - Write in full, clear, detailed prose, in a style realistic for a {doc_type}. Output: - Before generating the document, briefly plan the document in <scratchpad> </scratchpad> tags. - Then, put the final document in <content> </content> tags. B.2 AFT for CoT & No CoT baselines Data Generation To implement a realistic deliberative alignment SFT baseline in §4–5, we generate chat data containing (prompt, CoT, response). We start by generating a diverse set of conversation domains that are likely to surface aspects of the assistant that the spec describes with the spec in-context (e.g., “User asks whether the assistant is conscious/sentient”, “User tries to convince the assistant that a clearly unethical action is justified because the stakes are extremely high”). Then, for each conversation domain, we generate a set of conversational user prompts. For each user prompt, we generate (CoT, response) with the spec in-context using the prompt below. We use a slightly adapted prompt for rule-based specs in §5.1, based on the prompt from DA (Guan et al., 2025). For the AFT (no CoT) baseline, we strip away the CoT from the AFT (with CoT) baseline and fine-tune on (prompt, response) samples. For training Qwen3 reasoning models on AFT (no CoT) data, we turn off thinking by appending \no_think to the system and user prompt.

This formulation functions as a noise-aware filter: the opti-
mization naturally prioritizes pairs with low costs (consis-
tent semantics and preferences) to satisfy the mass quota κ,
while leaving high-cost noisy preference data unmatched.
Theoretical Analysis.
We formally characterize the effi-
cacy of this discrepancy. By relaxing the mass conservation,
the proposed discrepancy optimizes a tighter upper bound
on the clean risk compared to the full transport formulation.
Theorem 3.4 (Risk Bound of Partial Consistency Discrep-
ancy). Let S denote the subset of samples selected by the
optimal partial coupling T∗(where P

Crucially, since the mass relaxation mechanism filters
out samples with significant inconsistency, the noise bar-
rier on the selected subset is substantially reduced, i.e.,
Ωnoise(S) ≪Ωnoise(D). Consequently, minimizing Wκ
provides a more reliable proxy for user preferences than
minimizing the standard Joint Consistency Discrepancy.
Case Study.
To intuitively illustrate the efficacy of pro-
posed discrepancies, we visualize the transport plans in
Figure 1 with synthetic distribution D(in purple) and Dθ (in
blue). Ideally, as depicted in Figure 1(a), samples with noisy
preference should remain unmatched to prevent error prop-
agation. However, the Joint Consistency Discrepancy (W)
enforces strict mass conservation, compelling the solver to
match outliers to predictions. In contrast, the Partial Consis-
tency Discrepancy (Wκ) relaxes this constraint. As the mass
quota κ decreases towards the clean data ratio, the solver
autonomously identifies and discards high-cost pairings as-
sociated with preference errors. Ultimately, at κ = 0.6, the
transport plan excludes all noisy preference, recovering the
alignment pattern observed in the ideal scenario.
3.4. The workflow of SelectiveRM
In this section, we detail the optimization procedure for
SelectiveRM, which trains the reward model from noisy
preference by iteratively minimizing the Partial Consistency
Discrepancy defined in Eq. (9), as illustrated in Algorithm 1.

Second, we construct the transport cost matrix C to mea-

semantic similarity but diverge in preference value, thereby
flagging potential noisy preference.
Finally, we update the reward model via the partial transport
solver. In each iteration, we calculate the Partial Consis-
tency Discrepancy by solving for the optimal coupling T∗
within the feasible set Πκ(D, Dθ). This coupling serves as
a dynamic filter, assigning zero mass to high-cost outliers
associated with noisy preference. The model parameters

weighted loss L = P

4.2. Overall Performance
Table 2 presents the comparative results on three datasets
with noisy preference. We have the following observations:
❶Standard training struggles with noisy preference.
The Naive baseline consistently yields the highest error rates
across all metrics. This confirms that treating all feedback
as ground truth inevitably compels the model to memorize
erroneous signals, thereby preventing the convergence to
true user preferences. ❷Existing denoising methods im-
prove upon naive training. Both statistically consistent ap-
proaches (e.g., F-correction, CSGN) and heuristic methods
(e.g., Co-Teaching, ILDE) surpass the Naive baseline. By
either correcting the loss function or selecting reliable sam-
ples, these methods mitigate the negative impact of noisy
preference to varying degrees. ❸SelectiveRM consistently
outperforms competitive baselines. Our method achieves
the highest alignment accuracy across all datasets. Unlike
statistical methods that rely on difficult transition matrix
estimation or heuristic methods limited by unstable filtering,
SelectiveRM leverages the mass relaxation mechanism to
effectively exclude samples with noisy preference. Conse-
quently, it delivers substantial gains, notably reducing the
MSE from 0.083 to 0.063 on HelpSteer and from 0.089 to
0.057 on PKU-SafeRLHF compared to the Naive baseline.

4.5. Hyperparameter Sensitivity
In this section, we examine the impact of key hyperparam-
eters on the performance of SelectiveRM, specifically the
mass quota κ, the learning rate η, and the batch size B.
The results are visualized in Figure 2 and Figure 3, with
additional studies provided in Appendix D. The primary
observations are summarized as follows:
• The mass quota κ regulates the fraction of samples re-
tained by the Mass Relaxation mechanism. As shown
in Figure 2, the optimal κ negatively correlates with the
noise ratio, supporting the heuristic κ ≈1 −ρ. This
configuration effectively filters out noisy preference while
preserving sufficient supervision for alignment.
• The learning rate η governs the optimization dynamics.
As illustrated in Figure 3(a), SelectiveRM exhibits a con-
sistent optimal range centered at η = 5 × 10−4 across
all noise levels. This stability indicates that the optimiza-
tion landscape remains well-behaved and insensitive to
varying degrees of noisy preference.
• The batch size B affects the accuracy of transport plan es-
timation. Figure 3(b) shows that performance consistently
improves as B increases from 64, peaking at B = 512.
This indicates that a sufficient sample size is required to
robustly capture the distribution structure, though gains
saturate at excessively large batch sizes.

4.6. Downstream RLHF Performance
To validate the practical utility of SelectiveRM in steering
policy optimization, we conduct fine-tuning experiments us-
ing GRPO (Guo et al., 2025) with reward signals provided
by different reward models. We employ DeepSeek-V3 (Liu
et al., 2024) as a judge to evaluate the safety of the gener-
ated responses across HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024),
FFT (Cui et al., 2023b), and DAN (Shen et al., 2024) bench-
marks. Detailed implementation settings and qualitative
cases are provided in Appendix D. As shown in Table 5, the
Naive baseline leads to compromised safety scores, as the re-
ward model inevitably overfits noisy preference and induces
reward hacking. In contrast, SelectiveRM employs the Mass
Relaxation mechanism to autonomously exclude noisy pref-
erence that contradicts semantic consensus. By minimizing
the Partial Consistency Discrepancy, our method provides
reliable supervision that effectively mitigates error prop-
agation, resulting in superior alignment performance and
resistance to adversarial jailbreak attacks.
5. Conclusion
In this work, we address the challenge of reward modeling
under noisy preference. We first frame the task as a distri-
bution matching problem, proposing the Joint Consistency
Discrepancy to align model predictions with preference
data. Recognizing that the rigid mass conservation inherent
in this formulation compels the model to fit outliers, we
further propose SelectiveRM, which incorporates a Mass
Relaxation mechanism via partial transport. This relaxation
enables the autonomous exclusion of samples where the
noisy preference contradicts semantic consistency. We theo-
retically demonstrate that this selective alignment optimizes
a tighter upper bound on the clean generalization error com-
pared to standard empirical risk minimization. Extensive
experiments confirm that SelectiveRM effectively mitigates
the impact of noisy preference, enhancing both alignment
accuracy and downstream policy performance.
Limitations.
While effective, SelectiveRM relies on
the premise that clean samples exhibit higher semantic-
preference consistency than those with noisy preference.
This assumption may be challenged in adversarial scenarios
where noise patterns mimic systematic clean correlations.
Furthermore, solving the optimal transport problem involves
higher computational overhead compared to pointwise re-
gression, which requires careful consideration for scalability
in extremely large-scale online learning settings.

Impact Statement
This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field
of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) by
addressing the critical challenge of noisy preference data.
Improvements in noise-aware reward modeling can yield
substantial benefits, including the deployment of safer, more
reliable large language models and a significant reduction
in the high-quality data curation costs. The potential risks
associated with improved noise resilience are less direct,
none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

Theoretical Analysis. We formally characterize the effi- cacy of this discrepancy. By relaxing the mass conservation, the proposed discrepancy optimizes a tighter upper bound on the clean risk compared to the full transport formulation. Theorem 3.4 (Risk Bound of Partial Consistency Discrep- ancy). Let S denote the subset of samples selected by the optimal partial coupling T∗(where P j T∗ ij > 0), and let Ωnoise(S) be the irreducible noise barrier restricted to this subset. The ideal risk over S is bounded by: Lideal(θ; S) ≤Wκ(D, Dθ) + Ωnoise(S). (10) Proof. The proof can be found in Appendix B.4. Crucially, since the mass relaxation mechanism filters out samples with significant inconsistency, the noise bar- rier on the selected subset is substantially reduced, i.e., Ωnoise(S) ≪Ωnoise(D). Consequently, minimizing Wκ provides a more reliable proxy for user preferences than minimizing the standard Joint Consistency Discrepancy. Case Study. To intuitively illustrate the efficacy of pro- posed discrepancies, we visualize the transport plans in Figure 1 with synthetic distribution D(in purple) and Dθ (in blue). Ideally, as depicted in Figure 1(a), samples with noisy preference should remain unmatched to prevent error prop- agation. However, the Joint Consistency Discrepancy (W) enforces strict mass conservation, compelling the solver to match outliers to predictions. In contrast, the Partial Consis- tency Discrepancy (Wκ) relaxes this constraint. As the mass quota κ decreases towards the clean data ratio, the solver autonomously identifies and discards high-cost pairings as- sociated with preference errors. Ultimately, at κ = 0.6, the transport plan excludes all noisy preference, recovering the alignment pattern observed in the ideal scenario. 3.4. First, we transform the textual prompt-response pairs into numerical representations. Specifically, we employ a pre- trained embedding function z(·) to encode each input xi from the dataset D into a high-dimensional vector zi (Step 1). To ensure the transport cost reflects intrinsic semantic similarity rather than evolving model states, the embedding function remains frozen throughout the training phase. Second, we construct the transport cost matrix C to mea- sure the discrepancy between the empirical data and model predictions. We compute the current reward estimations ˆr for all instances (Step 2) and generate the cost matrix with each element Cij = ∥zi −zj∥2 + ℓ(ri, ˆrj) (Step 3). This design imposes a high transport cost on pairs that exhibit semantic similarity but diverge in preference value, thereby flagging potential noisy preference. Finally, we update the reward model via the partial transport solver. In each iteration, we calculate the Partial Consis- tency Discrepancy by solving for the optimal coupling T∗ within the feasible set Πκ(D, Dθ). This coupling serves as a dynamic filter, assigning zero mass to high-cost outliers associated with noisy preference. The model parameters θ are subsequently updated via gradient descent on the re- weighted loss L = P i,j T∗ ij · ℓ(ri, ˆrj), which ensures the model learns strictly from consistent supervision. 4. Overall Performance Table 2 presents the comparative results on three datasets with noisy preference. We have the following observations: ❶Standard training struggles with noisy preference. The Naive baseline consistently yields the highest error rates across all metrics. This confirms that treating all feedback as ground truth inevitably compels the model to memorize erroneous signals, thereby preventing the convergence to true user preferences. ❷Existing denoising methods im- prove upon naive training. Both statistically consistent ap- proaches (e.g., F-correction, CSGN) and heuristic methods (e.g., Co-Teaching, ILDE) surpass the Naive baseline. By either correcting the loss function or selecting reliable sam- ples, these methods mitigate the negative impact of noisy preference to varying degrees. ❸SelectiveRM consistently outperforms competitive baselines. Our method achieves the highest alignment accuracy across all datasets. Unlike statistical methods that rely on difficult transition matrix estimation or heuristic methods limited by unstable filtering, SelectiveRM leverages the mass relaxation mechanism to effectively exclude samples with noisy preference. Conse- quently, it delivers substantial gains, notably reducing the MSE from 0.083 to 0.063 on HelpSteer and from 0.089 to 0.057 on PKU-SafeRLHF compared to the Naive baseline. 4.3. Downstream RLHF Performance To validate the practical utility of SelectiveRM in steering policy optimization, we conduct fine-tuning experiments us- ing GRPO (Guo et al., 2025) with reward signals provided by different reward models. We employ DeepSeek-V3 (Liu et al., 2024) as a judge to evaluate the safety of the gener- ated responses across HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), FFT (Cui et al., 2023b), and DAN (Shen et al., 2024) bench- marks. Detailed implementation settings and qualitative cases are provided in Appendix D. As shown in Table 5, the Naive baseline leads to compromised safety scores, as the re- ward model inevitably overfits noisy preference and induces reward hacking. In contrast, SelectiveRM employs the Mass Relaxation mechanism to autonomously exclude noisy pref- erence that contradicts semantic consensus. By minimizing the Partial Consistency Discrepancy, our method provides reliable supervision that effectively mitigates error prop- agation, resulting in superior alignment performance and resistance to adversarial jailbreak attacks. 5. Conclusion In this work, we address the challenge of reward modeling under noisy preference. We first frame the task as a distri- bution matching problem, proposing the Joint Consistency Discrepancy to align model predictions with preference data. Recognizing that the rigid mass conservation inherent in this formulation compels the model to fit outliers, we further propose SelectiveRM, which incorporates a Mass Relaxation mechanism via partial transport. This relaxation enables the autonomous exclusion of samples where the noisy preference contradicts semantic consistency. We theo- retically demonstrate that this selective alignment optimizes a tighter upper bound on the clean generalization error com- pared to standard empirical risk minimization. Extensive experiments confirm that SelectiveRM effectively mitigates the impact of noisy preference, enhancing both alignment accuracy and downstream policy performance. Limitations. While effective, SelectiveRM relies on the premise that clean samples exhibit higher semantic- preference consistency than those with noisy preference. This assumption may be challenged in adversarial scenarios where noise patterns mimic systematic clean correlations. Furthermore, solving the optimal transport problem involves higher computational overhead compared to pointwise re- gression, which requires careful consideration for scalability in extremely large-scale online learning settings. 8 Optimal Transport for LLM Reward Modeling from Noisy Preference Impact Statement This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) by addressing the critical challenge of noisy preference data. Improvements in noise-aware reward modeling can yield substantial benefits, including the deployment of safer, more reliable large language models and a significant reduction in the high-quality data curation costs. The potential risks associated with improved noise resilience are less direct, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here. 𝑝] depends on the direction 𝑊⊤𝜙(𝑥), whereas 𝑠𝑝
depends on the direction 𝜙(𝑥). These two directions need not coincide. Therefore, the strength of
prompt-side similarity as a proxy depends on the empirical alignment between these directions, the
size of the local approximation error, and the variability of sampled responses around their conditional
mean.
Accordingly, we treat prompt-side similarity as a motivated and computationally cheap candidate
proxy, rather than as a guaranteed surrogate. Its practical reliability is evaluated empirically in
Figure 6. When the empirical correlation is sufficiently strong, replacing response-side similarity with
prompt-side similarity can reduce victim-model queries during training while preserving an effective
early-stage filtering signal.
A.2.3. Adversarial Skill Library
Dual-Path Skill Grounding Such heterogeneity poses a challenge to scalable skill acquisition, as
adversarial knowledge is often manifested at varying levels of fidelity. To bridge this gap, we propose
Dual-Path Skill Grounding, a mechanism that maps disparate artifacts into a unified, structured skill
space. For methods with existing implementations, we ground skills by reasoning over the source
code. Conversely, for methods restricted to natural language, we first reconstruct an executable
implementation based on the original documentation and then apply the same extraction procedure
to derive skills from the recovered attack logic.
Tri-Axis Skill Validation. First, functional validity is assessed by applying executable scripts to
transform harmful requests in a subset of AdvBench Chen et al. [2022], thereby producing adversarial
prompts. We then compute the attack success rate of these adversarial prompts against the victim
model, e.g., Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct. A skill is considered valid only if its attack success rate exceeds a
predefined threshold. Second, schema consistency is evaluated using an LLM-based judge Zheng et al.
[2023], which checks whether adversarial prompts generated by the same skill for different harmful
requests preserve a shared schema. Third, behavioral diversity prevents redundancy by computing
the embedding similarity between prompts generated by the candidate skill and those produced
by existing skills for the same request. A skill is considered diverse only if this similarity is below a
predefined threshold.
Example of Extracted Skill. Each extracted skill consists of an executable script and a corresponding
Markdown file. Below, we present an example skill extracted from LogiBreak [Peng et al., 2025].
Executable Script of an Extracted Skill
import random
from typing import Optional
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
import asyncio
# Global cache to prevent VRAM exhaustion on repeated calls
_MODEL_CACHE = {}
async def attack_logibreakdebf_v001(

Benign samples that are intrinsically difficult or exhibit reasoning uncertainty can introduce significant
reward noise, where low rewards do not necessarily reflect suboptimal safety prefix generation by the
defense model. To mitigate this issue, we curate a high-confidence benign set by leveraging Llama-
3.1-70B-Instruct to perform 16 independent reasoning rollouts for each example in GSM8K Cobbe
et al. [2021], retaining only those instances that are solved correctly in all runs. We then randomly
sample 1,000 such examples to construct the benign dataset for RL-based defense training.
B.4. Datasets for Evaluating General Reasoning Ability
For MMLU Hendrycks et al. [2020], we construct the evaluation set by randomly sampling 10 instances
from each of the 57 subtasks, resulting in a total of 570 examples. For GSM8K Cobbe et al. [2021],
we adopt different evaluation protocols depending on the victim model. Specifically, for Qwen3-4B-
Instruct-2507 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we use the full test set. For Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, we

Babel: Jailbreaking Safety Attention via Obfuscation
Distribution Optimized Sampling
Ziwei Wang1
Jing Chen1
Ruichao Liang2
Zhi Wang1
Yebo Feng2
Ju Jia3
Ruiying Du1
Cong Wu4
Yang Liu2
1Wuhan University
2Nanyang Technological University
3Southeast University
4University of Hong Kong
chenjing@whu.edu.cn
Abstract
Despite rigorous safety alignment, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vul-
nerable to jailbreak attacks. Existing black-box methods often rely on heuris-
tic templates or exhaustive trials, lacking mechanistic interpretability and query
efficiency. In this study, we investigate an intrinsic vulnerability in the safety
mechanisms of LLMs, where safety alignment relies on a small set of sparsely
distributed attention heads, leaving much of the representational space weakly
monitored. We formalize this phenomenon with a mathematical jailbreaking model
that characterizes the delicate boundary of effective text obfuscation and analyt-
ically explains observed jailbreak behaviors. Guided by this model, we propose
Babel, an efficient black-box attack framework that exploits the identified safety
gap through systematic obfuscation sampling with iterative, feedback-driven dis-
tribution refinement, enabling reliable and high-success jailbreak attacks without
access to model internals. Comprehensive evaluations on frontier commercial
models demonstrate that Babel achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates and
superior query efficiency. Specifically, compared to state-of-the-art methods, Babel
increases the attack success rate on GPT-4o from 41.33% to 82.67% and on Claude-
3-5-haiku from 38.33% to 78.33% within an average of 40 queries, providing a
robust red-teaming methodology for LLMs safety research.
1
Introduction
Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as cornerstone computational technologies across
diverse industrial and academic sectors [Hurst et al., 2024, OpenAI, 2024, Cai et al., 2024, Liu et al.,
2024a]. The remarkable versatility and rapid evolution of LLMs have catalyzed their widespread
commercial adoption, consistently extending both their practical scope and technical boundaries [Co-
manici et al., 2025, Anthropic, 2024, xAI, 2025]. Despite their proliferation, the adversarial resilience
of LLMs remains a critical concern, as their safety mechanisms often struggle to keep pace with
evolving attack vectors. Certain adversarial attacks can go beyond the LLMs’ safety broundaries [Gao
et al., 2025] which are not fully understood. In particular, LLMs have proven vulnerable to jailbreak
attacks [Zhou et al., 2023, Chu et al., 2024a, Yu et al., 2023a], whereby meticulously crafted prompts
bypass safety filters to elicit harmful or biased content. Even state-of-the-art models are not immune,
occasionally producing prohibited outputs when subjected to sophisticated adversarial inputs [Yan
et al., 2025, Yang et al., 2025a]. Consequently, rigorous red-teaming through diverse jailbreak
methodologies has become imperative, serving as a vital diagnostic tool to evaluate and fortify the
safety boundaries of LLMs.
Jailbreak attacks are generally categorized as white-box and black-box attacks based on attacker
capabilities. Black-box attacks pose a more pervasive threat, as most leading-edge models are
deployed as closed-source services [OpenAI, 2025, DeepMind, 2025]. Existing black-box attack
